title: The Struck Bell
author: Aldith Sulion, Sayer of the Circle, after the Oroth
body:
# The Struck Bell

*The first account, set down plainly, with the objections at the end where they belong.*

The world is the ringing of a bell that was struck once, before time, and has been fading ever since. Sound is being. This is not an image. Where the ringing is loud there is warmth, weight, colour and duration; where it has thinned, things go still, and grey, and at last **unsaid**.

You may test this yourself and I recommend it, since you will not believe me otherwise. Go into any deep place. Speak at your ordinary volume. Your voice will not carry as far as it does in a field, and you will attribute this to the stone, and you will be wrong, because it does not carry as far as it does in a *cellar* either, and a cellar is stone. Then count how long a struck note hangs. In the Undercroft, under the city, a hand-bell rings for four seconds. In the Drowned Nave the same bell rings for one. In the Cantor's Seat, by three accounts I have from the Order and do not doubt, it does not ring at all: it makes a sound and the sound is over.

The Builders understood this better than we do, and their failure is the most valuable document we possess. They raised the **Harmonies**: cathedral-machines the size of towns, tuned to sustain the note against its fading. They spent an age on it. The fused roads, the hinge-less doors, the twelve colossi of the Choir, Tollmere's foundation which no one has ever dug through — all of it is one engineering project, and the project failed, and they are gone from the record, and their greatest work is still running.

That is the part my colleagues refuse to sit with. The **Cantor's Seat** did not fail. It holds a note. It holds the *wrong* note, a fifth below where the Choir's ring was cut to sound, and it has held it for a thousand years, and while it holds it the dead in the deep places do not finish. They are not cursed. They are **sustained**, in the way a finger on a string sustains a string: not kindly, not cruelly, simply held.

The Cracked Toll has begun to hum. A bell that has been silent since it fell is now sounding a half-step under a tine of Oroth stone found in its crown. Two objects made to agree have stopped agreeing, and one of them is forty metres of bronze and the other is the world.

## Objections, as I am obliged to record them

**First.** My account cannot explain why a village whose people talk about one another keeps its colour, and one whose people do not, does not. Gossip is not sound in any sense I can measure. It does not carry past the next field. It works anyway. I have measured eleven villages over nine years and the correlation is not in doubt and I have no mechanism, none, and I teach the Bell regardless, because an account that fails at one thing and predicts nine is worth more than a warm feeling that predicts nothing.

**Second.** Cresswell says that if being is sound, the deaf should dwindle. They do not. I have no answer. He knows I have no answer. He raises it at every council and I have come to look forward to it.

title: The Candle Book
author: kept by the hearths of Hearthvale; this copy written out by Bennick Cresswell
body:
# The Candle Book

*What Vale mothers tell children, written down at last by a man who should know better.*

The world is a candle. The sun is its flame, and every hearth in every house is a small copy of it, and a flame goes out when nobody tends it.

That is the whole account. The rest is examples, and I have hundreds, and I shall give you the ones that can be checked.

**Tending** is everything done with care and in company. Cooking. Mending. Painting a door. Naming a child on Naming Day in front of the whole village so that eighty people have said the name aloud before the child can say it. Carrying a loaf to a neighbour's door, which in the Vale counts as a sentence spoken, and three loaves as a friendship. And talk: talk about who is ill, who is courting, who has been at the cider, who has not been seen since Tollday. Gossip is a kind of prayer. I say this in a building where it gets me laughed at, and then I go down to the quay and the fishers tell me who has fallen out with whom, and I am at my devotions.

A person nobody speaks of goes quiet. Then one day they are not there, and nobody can say when, and — this is the part to attend to — nobody can say *who*. Ask in Merrowby about the woman who sold hedge-honey on the end stall. They will remember the honey. They bought it for years. They cannot tell you her face.

The proof of this account is not in my keeping. It is in a book at Wardens' Rest that no Sayer wrote, kept by a militia who have never read a word of mine, and every line in it is a settlement that stopped being talked about and then stopped being findable. They read those names aloud once a week. They will tell you it is custom. I tell you it is the only working machine anyone in Wickmere has ever built against the Dwindling, and it is operated by an old man at a bell at five in the morning.

## Where it fails

At the largest objects in the world, which is embarrassing for a man who talks as much as I do.

The Builders' works are cold, tended by nobody for a thousand years, gossiped about by no one, and **standing**. By my account the Cantor's Seat should have gone before Larkstead did. Larkstead is gone. The Seat is not. I have tried the argument that the Cantor is himself the tending — one soul doing the work of a village, for ten centuries — and Sulion took it apart in four sentences in front of nineteen students, and she was right, and I bought her a drink.

So: tend your hearth, say your neighbour's name, and know that this account, which is true in every kitchen in Hearthvale, is refuted by the largest building in the south. Both. At once. That is where we all are.

title: The Long Breath
author: Dunna ko-Kharrow, memory-keeper, set down for the Sayers at their request and against her own judgement
body:
# The Long Breath

*You asked me to write it. Writing is how your people forget slowly. Here it is.*

Something vast breathed the world out. It is now breathing in. What lies nearest the mouth goes first: the very old, the very deep, the forgotten.

I will give you evidence and not poetry, because you have enough poetry and none of it is ours.

**The order holds.** The oldest places fail first. Not the emptiest, not the poorest, not the furthest from a road — the oldest, in order, across six regions and four peoples who do not talk to each other and have no reason to agree. Greyfold before Larkstead. The Choir before Greyfold. The deep places before either. Any of your Sayers may check this in an afternoon with the Wardens' book and a clan roll and they have not, in ninety years, because checking is slower than lecturing.

**The giants.** They raised these mountains and they were breathed in long ago, and their bones are still here. That is what is left when a thing is taken back but its weight is not. You may walk through a ribcage two valleys east of my hold. It is eleven yards high. Stand in the skull at the far end and shout, and the shout comes back, and it comes back wrong, and every child in Kharrow has done it and none of them can tell you how it is wrong.

**The rope.** We keep long memories because memory is a hand on the rope. Not a prayer — a hand, on a rope, and the rope is going out, and there are seven clans holding it and singing so that we all pull at once. Four hundred lines, every morning, before food, by whoever keeps the memory. It is not art; art you may improve. If I improve the Rope-Song, someone's grandmother is gone by Tollday and there is nobody to notice but me.

Your Circle calls this sentiment. It is the only intervention anyone has ever demonstrated to work. It works badly. It is what we have.

## The hole

There should be eight verses. There are seven.

You will not find a gap written anywhere, because there is no gap in a song; there is only a place where the singer breathes. The eighth breath is longer than the others. Every memory-keeper for a thousand years has taken it. None of us has ever been able to say why and all of us can say exactly how long.

What we have: a clan went down into the Choir when the Choir was new, to sing with the Builders. They did not come back. What came up the shaft at Oskeld afterwards is their weight without their name, and it walks, and half this hold will tell you it is not a person and the other half will not say so in front of children.

## Where it fails

The Seat. If the oldest and deepest goes first, the Cantor's Seat should have been the first mouthful, and it is the one thing in the basin that has not gone. My account has a hole in it the shape of the largest object in the south. Your Ondrael says the same and says it first in every lecture, which is why she is the only one of you I answer letters from.

title: The Going Out
author: said on the boards at Isseva; written down by Tessane, Sayer of the Tide, in the eleven days she stayed
body:
# The Going Out

*I asked the elders of Isseva for their account. They asked me to sit down. Eleven days later this is what I had, and I have not tidied it, because the tidying is where their meaning goes.*

The world is a shore, and the Dwindling is the tide going out.

What is left on the sand is strange and beautiful and does not belong to the air. That is what the Sayers call the deep places, into which we go with lamps and out of which we come with opinions. The reedfolk go into them rarely, take what is useful, and do not theorise.

Things return with the flood. This is the part my Circle will seize on, so let me put it exactly as it was put to me, by a woman of sixty who had buried thirty-one people in the water: *some here believe the flood is coming and the drowned will walk. I do not believe it. I have never said so at a burial and I never shall.*

That sentence is the account. Not the flood — the patience, kept honestly, by people who know what it is worth.

**They build on stilts**, which is a way of agreeing with water rather than arguing with it. **They fish what is stranded**, which is a way of saying that a world going out leaves things worth having. **They put their dead on the water with a lantern** and do not go back to look, because the dead are finished, and that is the entire point of the ceremony. The eldest counts the lanterns still burning at first light. Not for the dead. Because a person should know how many small lights are still going in the direction they cannot see.

## Two things the Circle should not be allowed to ignore

**First.** *Isse* is water in Sedgish. *Isse* is water in Oroth. The reedfolk are supposed to have had no contact with the Builders whatsoever. Every Sayer I have put this to has looked at the ceiling. I have now put it to eleven.

**Second, and this is why I stayed the eleven days.** The tide takes everything back in its time — everything, and out here that is a comfort and not a threat. And there is one thing the tide does not reach, and it is in the south, and it is a note.

A held thing does not rot. That sounds like a blessing until you have watched a man hold his father's hand for three days after his father was dead. A held thing does not rot and it does not rest. Whatever sits in the Builders' Seat with its fist closed has been holding something for a thousand years, and this account says: *open the hand*. Not because the hand is wicked. Because the thing in it is tired.

## Where it fails

There has never been a flood. Not in any record, theirs or ours. I said so on the boards, kindly, on the third day, and the answer I was given was: *no. There has not.*

My account of their account is therefore this. It has never predicted anything. It has kept a town from despair for four hundred years. Those are not the same and they have had longer to sit with the difference than I have.

It is also the only one of the four that nobody has seriously tried to disprove, because nobody thought it worth the boat fare.
